edges.description: Neutrophil-predominant effusions loculate more, and loculation is associated with persistent pleural thickening. This is an association, not a demonstrated causal chain.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines increase pleural capillary permeability.
The Th1 response organises into granulomas in the parietal pleura.
Interferon-gamma-producing T cells control the bacilli, which keeps the effusion paucibacillary.
edges.target: Paucibacillary Containment with Persistent Viable Bacilli

edges.description: The pleural inflammation can leave fibrosis, thickening and adhesions.
The pleural inflammatory response produces an acute febrile illness.
Inflamed parietal pleura causes pleuritic chest pain.
Cough accompanies the pleural inflammation; coexisting parenchymal disease may contribute.
Constitutional symptoms are less common than the acute triad.
Night sweats are a less common constitutional symptom.
Leaked protein-rich fluid accumulates as an exudate.
Lymphocytic pleuritis and granulomas impair pleural fluid reabsorption.
Reduced clearance adds to the fluid that accumulates.
Without treatment, the persisting infection later causes active pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis in most patients.

nodes.description: Adjunctive prednisolone is not routinely recommended. In a Cochrane review of six trials (590 participants), corticosteroids may shorten resolution of the effusion and reduce residual effusion and pleural changes (low certainty), with no shown benefit on long-term lung function. Adverse events leading to discontinuation were more frequent, and in the trial in HIV-positive people Kaposi sarcoma occurred only in the steroid group, a caution against their use with HIV.

evidence.snippet: The risk of adverse events that led to discontinuation of the trial drug was higher in people with pleural TB receiving corticosteroids (RR 2.78, 95% CI 1.11 to 6.94; 587 participants, 6 trials, low certainty evidence).
cases of Kaposi's sarcoma were only seen in the corticosteroid group (with 6/99 cases in the steroid group compared to 0/98 in the control group)
There is no definitive evidence that steroids are beneficial in the management of pTB, and their routine use is not recommended

nodes.description: The same regimen as for pulmonary tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide (with ethambutol in current four-drug practice) for two months, then isoniazid and rifampicin for four months, under direct observation where adherence is a concern. Shorter regimens with fewer drugs have been studied because the disease is paucibacillary. Longer courses are used for complicated, loculated effusions and empyema, and have been suggested for empirically treated patients and people living with HIV, with limited supporting data. Drug-resistant disease is treated under drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis guidelines in an experienced centre. Treatment also prevents the later active tuberculosis that follows an untreated effusion.

evidence.snippet: The recommended treatment for TPE is a regimen with isoniazid, rifampin, and pyrazinamide for two months followed by four months of two drugs, isoniazid and rifampin.
A reasonable management strategy for pleural TB would be to initiate a four-drug regimen and perform a therapeutic thoracentesis in patients with large, symptomatic effusions.
A standard 6-month regimen is commonly used for drug-sensitive disease, with use of directly observed therapy where concern exists around potential compliance
Given the paucibacillary nature of pTB, some studies have explored the use of shorter regimens with fewer drugs
Longer regimens are commonly employed in complicated, loculated tuberculous effusions and in TB empyema

Extended treatment durations have also been suggested for subgroups of patients such as those receiving empiric therapy (as can frequently be the case in pTB) or PLHIV, although data supporting this strategy are limited
The treatment of drug-resistant pTB should follow international guidelines for the treatment of drug-resistant pulmonary TB and should be undertaken in an experienced centre.

nodes.description: In the first days neutrophils and monocytes enter the pleural space. About 10% of sampled tuberculous effusions are neutrophil predominant; these have higher smear and culture positivity and more loculation, and many become lymphocytic on repeat sampling.

evidence.snippet: While lymphocyte predominance is the most common finding in tuberculous effusions, ∼10% of sampled tuberculous effusions in human studies are neutrophil predominant

nodes.description: A unilateral (about 98% of cases), straw-coloured, protein-rich exudate that usually occupies less than two thirds of the hemithorax and is lymphocyte predominant in about 83-93% of effusions; early or neutrophil-predominant effusions are the exception.

nodes.description: HIV raises the rate of pleural involvement among people with tuberculosis. With low CD4 counts the local lymphocytic response is weaker, the pleural bacillary load higher (more smear- and culture-positive fluid), and the illness longer and more severe, with more constitutional symptoms and disseminated disease. Pleural ADA remains a useful marker even at low CD4 counts.

evidence.snippet: The incidence of pleural tuberculosis is higher in patients who are HIV positive.

evidence.reference_title: Evaluation of suspected tuberculous pleurisy: clinical and diagnostic findings in HIV-1-positive and HIV-negative adults in Uganda.
evidence.snippet: Of 156 individuals enrolled, 142 had tuberculosis, of whom 80% were HIV-positive. Among those with tuberculosis, HIV-positive patients bad a more severe and longer illness.
PLHIV with pTB often present later with constitutional symptoms and may have evidence of disseminated disease

nodes.description: Drainage with intrapleural fibrinolytics such as urokinase has been reported to reduce residual thickening, improve lung function and speed resolution in free-flowing and loculated effusions, but the optimal regimen is not established. No agent term is bound because the cited review names urokinase only as an example.

evidence.snippet: However, the optimal regimen has not yet been established.

nodes.description: Bacilli and mycobacterial antigens reach the pleural space, classically by rupture of a subpleural caseous focus; direct infection of the pleural space is now thought to start the cascade, rather than a purely hypersensitivity process.
nodes.id: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Entry into the Pleural Space

evidence.snippet: Tuberculosis is caused by the rupture of a pulmonary subpleural caseous focus, which releases mycobacterium into the pleural cavity

evidence.reference_title: Tuberculous pleural effusions: advances and controversies.
evidence.snippet: what was once thought to be an effusion as a result of a pure delayed hypersensitivity reaction is now believed to be the consequence of direct infection of the pleural space with a cascade of events including an immunological response

nodes.description: A less frequent constitutional symptom.

evidence.snippet: The most commonly reported symptoms are cough, chest pain and fever, and to a lesser extent, weight loss and night sweats

nodes.description: The Th1 response keeps the pleural bacillary load low, but viable bacilli persist. The effusion often resolves without treatment, yet the infection is not cleared, and higher smear and culture positivity with low CD4 counts shows that live bacilli are present.
nodes.id: Paucibacillary Containment with Persistent Viable Bacilli

evidence.snippet: these observations suggest that while the Th1 hypersensitivity reaction is central to the development and maintenance of the tuberculous effusion, it is likely that true pleural infection is present and persists
Pleural fluid cultures are positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in less than 40% and smears are virtually always negative.

nodes.description: Fibrinous organisation of the inflamed pleura produces septation, loculation, adhesions and residual pleural thickening, which can persist after treatment and impair lung function.

evidence.snippet: 50% of TPE patients have a thickened pleura as a result of the accumulation of fluid

nodes.description: Granulomas, often caseating, form in the parietal pleura. They are the histological basis of the diagnosis and, with the lymphocytic pleuritis, obstruct pleural lymphatic outflow.

evidence.reference_title: Tuberculous pleural effusion and tuberculous empyema.
evidence.snippet: the characteristic pleural involvement, granulomas with or without caseous necrosis, is evident in 56 to 80% of cases from samples obtained by percutaneous pleural biopsy

evidence.reference_title: Tuberculous pleurisy: a study of 254 patients.
evidence.snippet: Definitive diagnosis was based on the observation of caseous granulomas in pleural biopsy tissue samples in 79.8% of patients

nodes.description: Memory Th1 cells sensitised at the initial infection home selectively to the pleura and produce more interferon-gamma than their blood counterparts, compartmentalising the response. Interferon-gamma activates pleural macrophages, which release adenosine deaminase (the ADA2 isoenzyme). In sensitised guinea pigs, lymphocyte depletion prevents the effusion, so the lymphocytic influx is required for it.

evidence.snippet: The immediate cause of the effusion is a delayed hypersensitivity response to mycobacterial antigens in the pleural space.

The infiltrating lymphocytes seen in most tuberculous effusions are predominantly memory T-helper (Th)1 cells, presumably sensitised at the time of initial host infection, that selectively home to the infected pleural space
In a purified protein derivative-sensitised guinea pig model, lymphocyte depletion prevented the formation of a pleural effusion following injection of tuberculous protein into the pleural space
tuberculous effusions have high adenosine deaminase (ADA) activity, apparently due to high levels of the ADA isoenzyme ADA2, which is only found in monocytes and macrophages

nodes.description: Rare progression to frank tuberculous empyema, curated in full in Tuberculous_Empyema. No frequency is set because the available figure comes from a culture-confirmed referral series.

evidence.snippet: It represents a spectrum of disease that can variably self-resolve or progress to TB empyema with severe sequelae such as chronic fibrothorax or empyema necessitans

nodes.description: Residual pleural thickening after treatment, more than 2 mm in about half of patients and more than 10 mm in about a quarter in a randomised trial; it can impair lung function.

evidence.reference_title: Pigtail drainage in the treatment of tuberculous pleural effusions: a randomised study.
evidence.snippet: The incidence of RPT levels of more than 2 mm in the two groups was 50% and 51%, respectively.

evidence.reference_title: Pigtail drainage in the treatment of tuberculous pleural effusions: a randomised study.
evidence.snippet: The incidence of RPT of more than 10 mm in the group treated with pigtail drainage and anti-TB drugs was 26% compared with 28% in the group receiving drug treatment only.

nodes.description: Active pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis developing months to years after an untreated effusion has resolved. This is why the diagnosis must be made even though the effusion itself resolves.
nodes.id: Subsequent Active Tuberculosis After Untreated Pleurisy

evidence.snippet: if this diagnosis is not made the patient will recover only to have a high likelihood of subsequently developing pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis

nodes.description: Large, symptomatic effusions are drained for relief of dyspnoea. In a randomised trial, pigtail drainage added to chemotherapy shortened dyspnoea but did not reduce residual pleural thickening or improve forced vital capacity; evidence for routine early drainage is inconsistent.

evidence.reference_title: Pigtail drainage in the treatment of tuberculous pleural effusions: a randomised study.
evidence.snippet: The addition of pigtail drainage to an effective anti-TB regimen is not clinically relevant and does not reduce the level of RPT.
TB pleural effusions causing dyspnoea should be drained to provide symptomatic relief
